authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates the two-step sequence of neutron-induced fission of uranium-235, rendered as a left-to-right progression of nuclear space-filling/sphere-cluster models. A slow neutron strikes a U-235 nucleus, which absorbs it to form the short-lived intermediate U-236, depicted as an elongated, pinched nucleus outlined in red to convey its instability. The unstable nucleus rapidly splits into two smaller daughter nuclei — Ba-141 and Kr-92 — while simultaneously ejecting three neutrons and releasing a large burst of energy shown as a gold starburst labeled Energy. The balanced nuclear equation at the bottom confirms conservation of both mass number and atomic number across both steps. This figure introduces nuclear fission as a chain-reaction-capable process in which a single neutron absorption triggers the release of multiple secondary neutrons alongside an enormous quantity of energy, establishing the basis for both nuclear reactors and weapons.
authoredInteractions:
- Animate the step-by-step fission sequence: neutron strikes U-235, U-236 forms as a deformed nucleus, then splits releasing Kr-92, Ba-141, three neutrons, and an energy burst
- Click any product nucleus or particle: display its symbol, atomic number, mass number, and its role in sustaining a chain reaction
- Slider for chain reaction step: start from one fission event and show the three released neutrons each triggering additional fissions
authoredContext:
Many heavier elements with smaller binding energies per nucleon can decompose into more stable elements that have intermediate mass numbers and larger binding energies per nucleon—that is, mass numbers and binding energies per nucleon that are closer to the “peak” of the binding energy graph near 56 (see ). Sometimes neutrons are also produced. This decomposition is called fission , the breaking of a large nucleus into smaller pieces. The breaking is rather random with the formation of a large number of different products. Fission usually does not occur naturally, but is induced by bombardment with neutrons. The first reported nuclear fission occurred in 1939 when three German scientists, Lise Meitner, Otto Hahn, and Fritz Strassman, bombarded uranium-235 atoms with slow-moving neutrons that split the U-238 nuclei into smaller fragments that consisted of several neutrons and elements near the middle of the periodic table. Since then, fission has been observed in many other isotopes, including most actinide isotopes that have an odd number of neutrons. A typical nuclear fission reaction is shown in .

When a slow neutron hits a fissionable U-235 nucleus, it is absorbed and forms an unstable U-236 nucleus. The U-236 nucleus then rapidly breaks apart into two smaller nuclei (in this case, Ba-141 and Kr-92) along with several neutrons (usually two or three), and releases a very large amount of energy.

A diagram is shown which has a white sphere labeled “superscript, 1, subscript 0, n” followed by a right-facing arrow and a large sphere composed of many smaller white and green spheres labeled “superscript, 235, subscript 92, U.” The single sphere has impacted the larger sphere. A right-facing arrow leads from the larger sphere to a vertical dumbbell shaped collection of the same white and green spheres labeled “superscript, 236, subscript 92, U, Unstable nucleus.” Two right-facing arrows lead from the top and bottom of this structure to two new spheres that are also composed of green and white spheres and are slightly smaller than the others. The top sphere is labeled “superscript, 92, subscript 36, K r” while the lower one is labeled “superscript, 141, subscript 56, B a.” A starburst pattern labeled “Energy” lies between these two spheres and has three right-facing arrows leading from it to three white spheres labeled “3, superscript, 1, subscript 0, n.” A balanced nuclear equation is written below the diagram and says “superscript, 235, subscript 92, U, plus sign, superscript, 1, subscript 0, n, yield arrow, superscript, 236, subscript 92, U, yield arrow, superscript, 141, subscript 56, B a, plus sign, superscript, 92, subscript 36, K r, plus sign, 3, superscript, 1, subscript 0, n.”

Among the products of Meitner, Hahn, and Strassman’s fission reaction were barium, krypton, lanthanum, and cerium, all of which have nuclei that are more stable than uranium-235. Since then, hundreds of different isotopes have been observed among the products of fissionable substances. A few of the many reactions that occur for U-235, and a graph showing the distribution of its fission products and their yields, are shown in . Similar fission reactions have been observed with other uranium isotopes, as well as with a variety of other isotopes such as those of plutonium.

discrepancies: the default rendered figure is squeezed into the left portion of the viewport by a large control panel, making the main fission diagram much smaller than the source and not a clean drop-in replacement
most isotope labels and the bottom nuclear equation are too small and visually garbled in the screenshot; the source has large, clearly readable superscript/subscript nuclear notation
the U-236 unstable nucleus outline is a smoother red contour and does not closely scallop around the nucleon spheres the way the source outline does
the product labels for Kr-92, Ba-141, and 3 neutrons are present but poorly legible and less cleanly aligned with the particles than in the source
the optional chain-reaction generation control introduces a related but non-source visualization that competes with the original single fission-sequence figure
evaluation.notes: The main fission sequence, arrows, nuclei, energy burst, and balanced reaction are structurally recognizable, but the rendered default is too compressed and the key nuclear labels/equation are not legible enough to replace the source figure.
action_items: Increase the effective drawing area for the default figure or move/collapse the UI so the source-like diagram remains full-width and readable.
Redesign isotope labels and the bottom equation using larger grouped text or true baseline-shift styling so superscripts/subscripts remain clear at inline size.
Tighten label placement around Kr, Ba, emitted neutrons, and the bottom reaction so each annotation is visibly attached to the correct element without shrinking.
Make the red U-236 instability boundary more scalloped and closer to the outer nucleon contour to match the source.
plan_action_items: Keep the chain-reaction generation view secondary or optional; the primary default interaction should preserve the original neutron-induced fission sequence and equation.
